title: Why does a passing siren drop in pitch?
hook: The siren never changes. So why does it sound higher coming, and lower going?

knows: sirens sound higher as they come and lower as they go
doesNotKnow: that a moving source bunches its wavefronts ahead and spreads them behind

misconception: The siren itself changes pitch as it approaches or leaves.
objective: The learner can explain that the siren's motion bunches crests in front and spreads them behind, so the pitch you hear shifts even though the siren never changes.

claims.text: For a source moving at speed v toward or away from a still listener in still air, the heard frequency is f c / (c - v) approaching and f c / (c + v) receding.
claims.source: Doppler effect for a moving source; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 17.

claims.text: A 700 Hz siren at 25 m/s is heard at about 755 Hz head-on approaching and about 652 Hz receding.

Standing 3 m from the road, you hear about 754 Hz with the ambulance 20 m before you, about 704 Hz as it is beside you (that sound left a moment earlier, while still approaching), and about 653 Hz 20 m past you.
claims.source: Computed in Demo.tsx with retarded emission time tau from (x - v tau)^2 + 3^2 = (c tau)^2 and f' = f c / (c - v cos phi). Values at slider stops x = -80, -60, -40, -20, 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 m: 755.0, 755.0, 754.9, 754.5, 703.7, 653.0, 652.6, 652.5, 652.5 Hz. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-derived in node from heard(): -20 m 754.47 (stage shows 754), 0 m 703.74 (704), +20 m 653.01 (653); other stops 755.0, 755.0, 754.9, 652.6, 652.5, 652.5 match the source list.

claims.text: The siren's own pitch never changes; the driver hears 700 Hz throughout.
claims.source: Source and driver move together: no relative motion, no shift.

claims.text: The rings show sound sent out 0.1 s apart, centred where the ambulance was when it sent them; they bunch ahead and spread behind.
claims.source: Ring of age tau is centred at x - v tau with radius c tau; spacing ahead (c - v) x 0.1 = 31.8 m, behind (c + v) x 0.1 = 36.8 m. Only every 70th crest is drawn (illustrative spacing).

claims.text: Model: still air, sound at 343 m/s.
claims.source: Stated in the reveal. Sound speed in dry air at 20 C. (v2 removed the learner-visible sentence about standing close making the drop quick: no control showed it.) | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Speed of sound 343 m/s at 20 C in dry air (standard value, 343.2); stated as the model's assumption.

claims.text: Pitch in Hz is crests per second. Rings sent 0.1 s apart from a parked siren are 34.3 m apart; from the ambulance at 25 m/s they are 31.8 m apart ahead and 36.8 m behind, so ahead crests arrive 34.3 / 31.8 = 1.08 times as often, up to 755 Hz.
claims.source: Hz = cycles per second (SI). Parked spacing c x 0.1 = 34.3 m; ahead (c - v) x 0.1 = 31.8 m; behind (c + v) x 0.1 = 36.8 m. 34.3 / 31.8 = 1.079; 700 x 1.079 = 755 Hz (same as c2, 700 x 343 / 318). Computed from the same constants in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 34.3, 31.8, 36.8 m; 34.3/31.8 = 1.0786 -> '1.08'; 700 x 343/318 = 755.03. Stage caption is a separate claim (added c8).

claims.text: Each ring is a crest, sent 0.1 s apart. Hz = crests per second.
claims.source: Stage caption before the reveal. CONCERN: a 700 Hz siren sends crests 1/700 s (1.4 ms) apart, so rings 0.1 s apart are every 70th crest (Demo.tsx header comment and c5 say so); the caption says each ring is a crest. Suggest 'Each ring marks sound sent 0.1 s ago; a real 700 Hz siren sends 70 crests in that time.' Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check.

recall.question: A train horn sounds 400 Hz to the driver. Standing by the track as it rushes toward you, what do you hear?
recall.why: Coming toward you, the horn's crests bunch up and arrive more often, so the pitch you hear is higher; it drops as the train passes.
